editorNote: A window opens across the network at MIT, while Apple shrinks the II into a carryable package and VisiCorp tries to recover its business-software footing.
morningLine: The workstation screen is becoming a shared piece of the network.

lead.headline: MIT's Project Athena Opens a New Window
lead.dek: Robert Scheifler announces the X Window System, separating graphical programs from the screens that display them.
body: Robert Scheifler at MIT's Project Athena announced the X Window System on June 19, giving the laboratory's networked workstations a new way to draw and manage graphical displays. The first implementation was written for a VAX VS100, but its central idea reaches beyond a single machine.

X separates an application from the display on which its windows appear. A program can run on one computer while sending its graphical output across a network to another screen—an arrangement well suited to Athena, where students and researchers share computing resources rather than sit before isolated personal machines.

That division also gives workstation makers and software writers a common architectural problem to solve. Instead of every program owning the whole screen, a window system can let several tasks share it, move their output between machines and leave room for different user-interface conventions above the basic display machinery.

The announcement is modest beside a finished commercial product, but its network-first design makes it one of the week's most consequential experiments. Project Athena is building for a campus full of linked machines, and X suggests that the graphical desktop may belong as much to the network as to the computer on the desk.

stories.headline: VisiCorp Tries to Re-enter the Business-Software Race
body: VisiCorp used a June 18 product announcement to rebuild a business line battered by fierce competition. The company that turned VisiCalc into the early personal computer's defining spreadsheet introduced several products and presented the program as a return to the mainstream business market.

Among the announcements was a floppy-disk-based version of Visi On, the graphical office environment whose ambitions had been constrained by demanding hardware and a fast-moving IBM PC market. The new approach aims to put its visual shell and integrated tools within reach of more installed machines.

VisiCorp's comeback bid arrives while Lotus 1-2-3 and a widening field of IBM-compatible software redefine buyers' expectations. A pioneering name now has to prove that graphical presentation can be more than an expensive preview of tomorrow.

stories.headline: Apple IIc Packs the Apple II into 7.5 Pounds
body: Apple's IIc compresses the long-lived Apple II family into a 7.5-pound case with a built-in 5.25-inch disk drive. Inside are a 1.02 MHz 65C02, 128K of RAM and 16K of ROM; outside, ports serve a display, printer, modem, mouse, joystick and second drive.

The $1,295 machine is intended to travel, though it still needs an external screen and wall power for ordinary use. Apple says roughly 90 percent of about 10,000 Apple II programs should run on it, a compatibility promise that turns the enormous software shelf into its chief advantage.

A $199 green-phosphor monitor and $329 external drive make a fuller desk system, while a $99 mouse with MousePaint points toward Apple's increasingly graphical identity. The IIc is less a new software world than a familiar one folded into a smaller package.

stories.headline: Stolen Password Exposes the Fragility of Online Credit Files
body: The New York Times reported June 22 that a password used to reach credit files had been stolen, a concise warning about the vulnerability of records moving behind dial-up connections and shared credentials.

The incident shows how a single reusable secret can stand between an outsider and sensitive personal information. As businesses centralize records and make terminals more useful, identity checks and accountability become part of the system rather than an afterthought.

No named crew, handle or bulletin board is reliably identified in the available report. The lesson is institutional: online information is only as secure as the controls surrounding the password that opens it.

curiosity.headline: Apple Promises a $600 Flat Screen for the IIc
curiosity.summary: Apple previews an 80-column by 24-row low-power LCD intended to make the compact IIc genuinely portable.
curiosity.detail: Creative Computing reported the flat display was scheduled for fall 1984 at $600; paired with a battery pack, it would remove the need for a television or AC-powered monitor.
